heroTitle: Understanding it takes the shame out of it.
heroBody: Families spend years asking why someone will not simply stop. The answer is in how the brain has changed — and once you see that clearly, you can stop fighting the person and start treating the disease.
definitionNote: Classified as a chronic brain disorder by the American Society of Addiction Medicine and the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
definitionParas: Addiction is compulsive substance use or behaviour that continues despite harmful consequences. It takes hold when repeated engagement with a drug or an activity alters the brain's reward and self-control circuits, producing intense cravings and a real loss of control.

Tolerance builds with repeated misuse: larger amounts, or more frequent use, are needed for the same effect — which escalates the addiction on its own. Long-term use then becomes a cycle in which the substance is needed simply to avoid withdrawal, until it is prioritised above everything that once mattered.

marks.title: Impaired control
marks.body: Using more, or longer, than intended — and being unable to cut down or stop.

marks.title: Compulsive use
marks.body: Intense preoccupation with obtaining or using, making it the primary focus of daily life.

marks.title: Continued use despite harm
marks.body: Persisting through physical, psychological, social and financial consequences.

marks.title: Risky use
marks.body: Using in hazardous situations, or ignoring a high risk of personal harm.

typesIntro: Both work on the same reward circuitry, and both can dominate a life. We treat substance use disorders here; where a behavioural addiction is present alongside one, it is addressed in therapy.
substancesIntro: Compulsive use of chemical substances despite the damage to physical health, mental wellbeing and relationships.

substances.name: Alcohol
substances.body: One of the most widespread and socially accepted addictions, heavily affecting physical health and cognitive function.

substances.name: Nicotine and tobacco
substances.body: A highly addictive chemical reliance, driven by how fast nicotine acts.

substances.name: Opioids
substances.body: Prescription painkillers such as OxyContin and morphine, and illicit drugs including heroin and fentanyl — highly addictive, with severe overdose risk.

substances.name: Stimulants
substances.body: Cocaine, methamphetamine and prescription ADHD medications.

substances.name: Cannabis
substances.body: Can lead to cannabis use disorder: compulsive daily use despite the disruption it causes.

substances.name: Sedatives and hallucinogens
substances.body: Misuse of prescription tranquillisers, sleeping pills or hallucinogenic substances.

behavioursIntro: A compulsive urge to perform an activity for short-term pleasure or relief, continuing even as it does long-term harm.

behaviours.name: Gambling
behaviours.body: The only behavioural addiction officially recognised as a mental health disorder in the DSM-5.

behaviours.name: Internet and social media
behaviours.body: A growing compulsion to stay online, driven by the engagement triggers built into digital platforms.

behaviours.name: Video gaming
behaviours.body: Excessive, all-consuming gaming that damages work, relationships or personal wellbeing.

behaviours.name: Shopping
behaviours.body: Compulsive purchasing and overspending driven by the thrill of buying rather than any need.

behaviours.name: Food
behaviours.body: A compulsive relationship with highly palatable or sugary food, marked by intense cravings and overeating.

behaviours.name: Sex and pornography
behaviours.body: Uncontrollable urges, thoughts or behaviours around sexual activity or explicit material that interfere with daily functioning.

behaviours.name: Work
behaviours.body: An unhealthy obsession with working that leads to neglecting relationships, health and wellbeing.

dependencyTitle: Not the same thing — and the difference matters.
dependencyParas: A person can be dependent and never develop an addiction. A person can be addicted without being dependent on a substance. But once dependence sets in, the risk of addiction rises dramatically.
The distinction is control. Tolerance and withdrawal appear in both. In addiction, control over the substance is lost completely and it takes priority over everything else in the person's life.
whoThreshold: Symptoms present for at least 12 months — or continuous, daily use across the previous three months.
whoSigns: Impaired control over substance use or unhealthy behaviour
Placing more importance on use than on essential daily responsibilities
Continuing to use even as consequences begin to appear
Increasing tolerance — needing more to feel the same effects
Withdrawal symptoms during a period without the substance
causesTitle: There is no single cause. There is a combination.
causesIntro: Genetic, environmental and developmental factors together make some people far more vulnerable to the brain-altering effects of substances. None of them is a moral failing.

items.name: Genetics
items.body: Hereditary traits account for roughly half of a person's risk. A blood relative with a substance use disorder significantly raises your susceptibility.

items.name: Brain chemistry
items.body: Addictive substances hijack the reward system with massive dopamine surges. The brain desensitises, so more is needed for the same pleasure.

items.name: Mental health
items.body: Co-occurring depression, anxiety, ADHD or PTSD raise the risk — substances become a way to manage painful symptoms.

items.name: Trauma and stress
items.body: Physical, emotional or sexual abuse, especially in childhood, severely increases risk. So does chronic stress from financial instability or unstable housing.

items.name: Social surroundings
items.body: Growing up where substance use is normalised, or facing strong peer pressure, raises the likelihood of early experimentation.

items.name: Early exposure
items.body: Using highly addictive substances young changes the developing brain and greatly increases the chance of progressing to severe addiction.

items.name: The prefrontal cortex
items.body: The areas governing decision-making, judgement and self-control are still developing through adolescence, which makes young people especially prone to the risky, impulsive choices that lead to addiction.
